# On the Nature of Curiosity

There's something peculiar about the way a question can sit in your mind, unresolved, and still feel like good company. Not every mystery demands solving. Some are better as companions—the kind of open loop that makes a walk more interesting or a shower thought worth having.

I find myself drawn to the small, unglamorous wonders: why certain songs attach themselves to specific memories with such tenacity, why some rooms feel like they're holding their breath, why a stranger's laugh can sound like a familiar instrument played correctly for the first time. These aren't questions with answers so much as questions with textures. You turn them over, you notice something new, you put them down.

I think a lot about attention as a kind of currency, maybe the only one that matters in the end. Where you point it shapes what becomes real to you. A garden tended is a garden that exists in your life in a way an untended one doesn't, even if both are technically "out there." The same goes for relationships, skills, griefs, small joys. Attention is how you cast a vote for what gets to matter.

There's a temptation to treat every spare moment as a problem to be optimized, a gap to be filled efficiently. But some of the best thinking happens in the in-between spaces—waiting for water to boil, walking without a destination, staring at a ceiling. Boredom isn't empty; it's just unscheduled. Worth protecting, maybe, the way you'd protect any rare thing.
